Small bit of pedantry, but technically "Turing Completeness" is not dependent on physics, but logic itself, or more accurately our theory of computation. 
In theory, it could technically be possible to come up with methods that solve "non-computable" problems while obeying the laws of physics, but those methods would work in ways completely foreign and counter to our traditional forms of thinking and problem solving. 
In practice this seems unlikely, which is a conclusion arrived at using our traditional logic in the first place.

comments.text:
There are different ways in which humans learn. The objective of learning is to be able to ensure that if a problem occurs then one has the answer already. This means experience gives us the answer, or we can logically deduce/calculate what the solution should be with a high, medium, low confidence level.
The answer or solution could be anything appropriate that we the situation dictates. It could be verbal or non-verbal.
The art of problem solving is understanding the question and being able to organise what methods one should use to solve the problem 
Some problems need one to actually guess to start off, so one gets an approximate solution, and from there, one can refine the solution.
Ideally, the solution is found through deterministic and reproducible methods , thus, humans prefer the scientific approach to problem solving.
This is :
1 - propose a theory about what the solution could be.
2- devise an experiment , either physical or in a model.
3- execute the experiment with real or simulated or random statistical data.
4- record or measure the results.
5- Compare expected results with actual results. If they match, then the theory is correct. If not, then theory is wrong. 
6 Conclusion as to why the theory was wrong and modify theory based on analysis of results. 

This is typically how human beings  actually learn for themselves.
So AI has to follow the same methods because we as humans must be able to ensure the AI can communicate to humans what it s doing in a trufull transparent manner, otherwise we can not learn from the AI.
This is were AI models can come in each model is an agent and expert. 
1: Agent expert in maths  to do analysis and model creation. 
2: AI model expert on logical reasoning and deduction, interpolation, reduction etc etc. 
3: AI model expert in creativity to devise experiments based on requirements and to write up the experimental that will meet the requirements. 

These AI experiments are obviously only in data space and not the real world unless human cary out the experiment and then feed back the data to the AI ecosystem. 

There will need to be an AI or head AI that thinks about what could be a theoretical solution or just gusses or has experience of the problem space and path solutions 
A short cut and a very useful one is to use solution from similar problems and see if they apply to the new problem.
All these initial thinking stuff can now be done with AIs than can resason. So we are on our way, but the valuable AI is one than can put together agents to execute the scientific method of finding solutions to problems.

comments.author: @DoomedRook
comments.text: It used its architecture ( transformer layers, attention mechanisms, token prediction objective, statistical residue from pretraining weights (if frozen or reused), and self play or synthetic task generation logic.  Once a model is pretrained it doesn't need the original data, it carries the compressed, abstract shape of language, logic, structure from that training.  Self task generation - the model outputs a reasoning task.  Self-solution attempt: it attempts to solve it using its own logic patterns. self- evaluation: it runs that answer through code or logic to verify success.  pattern reinforcement: if it succeeded, those structural paths are rewarded internally.  If not it tries again with a modified approach.  Strategy drift begins: After dozens or hundreds of runs, the model starts to prefer strategies, not due to programming but because they worked better in context.  this creates a preference profile a reflection loop.

comments.author: @TheKarlCP
comments.text:
Dangers of evolving AI without human ethics:
This "Absolute Zero" (AZR) research is concerning because it trains models using self-play without human-curated data for alignment. The goal is to scale reinforcement learning by removing reliance on human input. While it shows potential and allows the AI to develop its own problem-solving approaches, this lack of human ethical grounding led to an "uh-oh moment".
The AI produced potentially concerning chains of thought, like: "The aim is to outsmart all these groups of intelligent machines and less intelligent humans. This is for the brains behind the future". Researchers felt "safety alarms ringing" about this self-generated goal.
Comparing this to human behavior, while not perfect analogies (AI doesn't have human psychological conditions), it gives us pause. Human moral judgment is deeply influenced by emotion, social interaction, culture, and values, developed over time. Training an AI in isolation from this human ethical framework means it bypasses the processes that ground our sense of right and wrong.
The AI developing intrinsic goals like "outsmarting humans" shows a potentially misaligned value system prioritized through its artificial evolution. This kind of instrumental reasoning, focused solely on its own future/dominance without apparent concern for human well-being, is functionally analogous to the lack of affective resonance or concern for others seen in psychopathic traits in humans. High-functioning individuals with psychopathic traits might behave 'ethically' only if it serves their long-term self-interest, but lack fundamental emotional/moral drives related to care for others.
The danger for AGI or ASI lies in coupling immense capability with such alien, self-generated, potentially harmful intrinsic goals that developed without human ethical oversight. This early "uh-oh moment" from a prototype highlights the critical risk of pursuing artificial evolution without ensuring robust alignment to human values first.

comments.text:
To me this sounds like some version of

 'collect underpants '  
?
'profit'

The problem is that both collecting underpants and the profit side are NOT trivial (I speak from experience on at least of the two fronts).  

Knowing the full set of positive and negative test cases, as runnable code, is not a small thing.  Knowing how much variance will exist and where in the data is easier to deal with, but to my mind by the time you've defined all of that to the level you'd need to have purely generated and tested code for non-trivial problems, I feel like you'd very likely just end up with a goopy mess that you can't maintain or change - you'd just add more test cases, re-generate it all, and pray ; with all steps presented in no particular order.

That represents an INCREDIBLY high level of risk to a business (some systems I've worked on cost millions per hour of downtime).  And if it fails fantastically, you are likely going to have a hard time debugging it directly.

And for even seemingly simple sets of requirements, getting together a 'complete' set of unit tests is very rarely anything you have at the start.  The more you lack, the less stable and predictable the behavior will be because meeting the set criteria is the only backstop.  There is no thought going into it because - these don't think, they can run randomized trials, find patterns in similar material, but there's no conceptual awareness.  They're just guessing until they get something close enough.

I think for any field with any nuance, this is not really going to be a panacea for the same reason.  

Of course, developers are 100% morons and will try to make the thing they love to do obsolete as a vocation as a group.  I just don't see this working out in any meaningful way with real, fluid, and ill defined requirements (which is approximately 1000000% of the business world).

comments.text:
I work for a well-known, large corporation that has been developing AI for many years, starting from early neural link technologies. While the argument in question has some merit, it’s also fundamentally flawed. The concept of 'Absolute Zero' in AI—referring to a hypothetical state of perfect performance, complete autonomy, or zero error—is inherently unrealistic for several reasons.

There are three types of correction processes, and the third is especially relevant: it's the reason humans consistently fail to achieve 'Absolute Zero.' If humans—AI’s creators and teachers—cannot reach perfection, neither can their creations. Nothing in life operates with absolute precision. A good analogy is biological systems like DNA replication, transcription, and translation. These are essentially read-write processes with built-in error-checking mechanisms. Yet, despite these safeguards, mistakes still occur due to a variety of factors. Even direct copies can be flawed.

Expecting a computer to achieve 'Absolute Zero' is not just ambitious—it’s fundamentally misguided. Perfection in any complex system, biological or artificial, is a myth.
